transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Hi, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Basically, what brings me in is that I just can't keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. 

It doesn't even matter if it's important, my focus just... slips. I do computer support, and lately I'll start tracing a client's network problem, and ten minutes later I'll realize I've reread the exact same log entries three times. And I still don't know what they actually say. It's getting really hard to get my work done.
How long has this difficulty concentrating been going on? Did it start suddenly, or has it been something you've always struggled with?

Well, the really serious trouble started about a year and ten months ago. I was fired from my old job back then. When that happened, I lost all the systems and routines I had built up over the years that used to keep me on track. Ever since then, without those structures in place, it's just been a constant struggle.
Over this past year and a half, how would you describe your mood overall? Have you been feeling sad, empty, or down most of the time?

No, not really. I mean, I definitely get frustrated with myself when I can't get my work done, but I wouldn't say I feel sad or down most of the time. Overall, my mood has been pretty normal. I don't feel empty or anything like that, just... annoyed that I'm struggling so much to focus.

You mentioned that losing your job and the routines you had built up made things harder. When you do have structure in place—like a clear deadline or someone checking in on your progress—are you still having trouble concentrating, or does that help you stay focused?

Well, deadlines used to help, but... lately, even with a hard deadline right in front of me, I still struggle. It's like my brain just won't engage, no matter how much pressure is on. I'll know I have to get something done by the end of the day, and I'll still find myself staring at the screen, totally zoned out. Someone checking in helps for a minute or two, but as soon as they walk away, I'm right back to losing my place. So, no, the structure doesn't really fix it anymore.

Looking back to your childhood and teenage years, before you lost your job—did you have similar trouble concentrating or staying focused on tasks, or is this difficulty with attention something that's really new for you in the past couple of years?

Well, no, it's definitely not new. I've always had these kinds of issues, even way back when I was a kid. My mother actually still jokes about it—she says that in grade school, all my report cards pretty much said the same thing. The teachers would write that I was bright, but I never stayed in my seat, I was always blurting out answers in class, and I'd constantly lose my homework. And the funny part is, I'd lose it even when I had actually done it. So, yeah, the trouble focusing and staying on track has always been there, it's just gotten a lot harder to manage lately.

Around the time your concentration problems got noticeably worse about a year and a half ago, did anything else happen health-wise? For example, did you have any head injuries, infections, start taking any new medications, or experience any significant changes in your physical health?

No, nothing like that. I didn't have any head injuries or get sick or anything. I haven't started any new medications either. My physical health has been pretty much the same as always. The only big change was losing my job and all the structure that came with it.

When you were in grade school, you mentioned not staying in your seat and blurting out answers—did you also feel like you had a lot of excess energy, like you needed to be moving around or doing something all the time, or was it more just that you couldn't help but interrupt and leave your seat in the moment?

Yeah, it was definitely the energy. It's always felt like... well, even when I'm supposed to just sit still and listen, it feels like there's a motor humming under my skin. I just get this constant feeling like I need to stand up, go check something, or just move on to the next problem right that second. So it wasn't just a quick impulse to interrupt—it was a real, physical need to be moving or doing something all the time.

You mentioned having that constant need to move around as a kid. Do you still experience that same physical restlessness and need to be moving now as an adult, or has that part gotten better over the years?

Yeah, it hasn't really gotten better. I still have that constant need to be doing something. Like, on my days off, I'll tell myself I'm just going to rest and take it easy. But I just can't. I end up bouncing around all day—going from a laptop repair, to working on the garage shelves, to checking a chess email, and then over to reorganizing cables. I just keep moving from one thing to the next, and by night... well, nothing is ever fully done.
